name: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies
description: Systems and measurements for user privacy: tracking, anonymization, private data sharing, and privacy on the web/mobile.
narrative:
The earliest USENIX Security work in this list reflects a moment when privacy research was splitting along two fronts: understanding what companies actually do with data, and tracking how sensitive data flows through software. On the policy side, "Polisis: Automated Analysis and Presentation of Privacy Policies Using Deep Learning" (2018) showed that the dense legal text users never read could be parsed and summarized automatically, and "Unveiling and Quantifying Facebook Exploitation of Sensitive Personal Data for Advertising Purposes" (2018) put hard numbers on how platforms monetize sensitive categories in the GDPR era. On the systems side, "Sensitive Information Tracking in Commodity IoT" (2018) extended classic taint-tracking to the new world of connected home devices, while "Towards Predicting Efficient and Anonymous Tor Circuits" (2018) carried forward the long-running concern of keeping anonymity-network users both fast and unlinkable.

Around 2019-2020 the field broadened in two directions. First, it confronted machine learning as both a privacy threat and a privacy tool: "Evaluating Differentially Private Machine Learning in Practice" (2019) gave a sober look at what differential privacy guarantees actually buy you, and "Fawkes: Protecting Privacy against Unauthorized Deep Learning Models" (2020) turned the tables by cloaking photos against facial recognition. Second, policy analysis matured from reading policies to catching them in lies, with "PolicyLint: Investigating Internal Privacy Policy Contradictions on Google Play" (2019) and "Actions Speak Louder than Words: Entity-Sensitive Privacy Policy and Data Flow Analysis with PoliCheck" (2020) cross-checking stated promises against real app behavior. This period also brought the human dimension into focus, with "The Tools and Tactics Used in Intimate Partner Surveillance" (2020) studying how privacy failures enable real-world abuse.

By 2021-2022 the cat-and-mouse game around network traffic and inference attacks intensified. Website fingerprinting moved from lab conditions toward realism in "Online Website Fingerprinting: Evaluating Website Fingerprinting Attacks on Tor in the Real World" (2022), while defenses and counter-defenses escalated through work like "Defeating DNN-Based Traffic Analysis Systems in Real-Time With Blind Adversarial Perturbations" (2021). Inference-style threats sharpened too, as "Are Your Sensitive Attributes Private? Novel Model Inversion Attribute Inference Attacks on Classification Models" (2022) and membership-inference work showed that deployed models leak more than expected.

Today the area sits at the intersection of generative AI, emerging hardware, and regulation. "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (2023) made vivid that modern generative models memorize and can regurgitate private training images, reframing the leakage problem for the AI era. New computing platforms brought new attack surfaces, exemplified by "Going through the motions: AR/VR keylogging from user head motions" (2023), and privacy-preserving learning continued to advance with "PrivateFL: Accurate, Differentially Private Federated Learning via Personalized Data Transformation" (2023). The throughline is clear: from auditing data practices and protecting anonymity, the field now also has to defend against models that both threaten privacy and must be trained privately, even as it tracks privacy onto entirely new devices.

milestones.note: grounded the hype around differential privacy by measuring what its guarantees actually deliver

milestones.note: flipped ML from privacy threat to defense by cloaking images against facial recognition

milestones.title: Online Website Fingerprinting: Evaluating Website Fingerprinting Attacks on Tor in the Real World
milestones.note: moved the long-running fingerprinting arms race from idealized labs to realistic conditions

milestones.title: Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models
milestones.note: showed generative models memorize and leak private training data, reframing privacy for the AI era
